Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Type of mechanics Dragon Keeper could be considered as a cooperative game, but with all the players being traitors. Each participant plays for himself, but they can be defeated together! In the game you will collect tiles (which depict different adventures trying to rob the dragon) to score points at the end. However, you will be dealt a guild card at the start, and will score negative points for any adventures from that guild you collect during the game. At each of your turns, you first move the dragon to pick up a tile from the row it's on, then move it again in the column and give a tile to the preceding player. If you give them a tile worth more than 2 you gain a gold. Some tiles include a special action. The tile that the following player will get depends on the position of the tile you have given, thus creating a strong interaction. The original guilds are secret, so you must deduce which ones are your opponents, to penalize them as much as possible. The level ends when the dragon can't land on any adventure tiles, and the player that causes this loses a gold. At the end of each level you must pay the dragon between 0 to 3 gold depending on how many tiles are left on the board, as depicted by the flames on your player board.. If you can't, you are eliminated. At the end of the third level each player must discard their highest stack of tiles (choose if two are equal) before paying the final tribute to the dragon. Then any tiles with the 'Release' special action is resolved before the final scores are calculated. [Rating: 2/10] Played it at Spiel with a group of 4 and we left after the first round because 2 of us almost felt physically ill because of how terrible it was. The mechanics are disjointed, annoying and don't really make sense (at least to me). Do not recommend.

[Rating: 3/10] A very forgettable game. I would much rather play a game like Butterfly which is simpler and more fun.

[Rating: 4/10] I really dislike the design of this game (the icons are not distinct enough) and I found the rules to be poorly written.  Even though it mentioned that some tiles have power, I took it to meant specific numbers (as in all except fives and sixes), rather than some of the ones through fours.  The actual gameplay is just move and collect, with a bit of majority and hidden scoring thrown in.  The multi level gimmick may be cool at first visually, but it doesn’t add anything interesting in the actual playing.

[Rating: 4/10] Probably just an unfortunate timing or sign of age or whatever, but I played Butterfly before playing this and it just pales in comparison to the former. There is not much meat here in the design and decision space. That means the game is light and easily approachable, but I guess that just means it is too light for me. I also don't love the title, art design, or rule book, so I guess this just isn't a design for me.

[Rating: 5/10] The idea of box within the box brings nothing to the gameplay, just a visual gimmick. Game itself is quite ok.

[Rating: 5/10] A so-so experience, but the designer really deserves credit for using the box in a creative manner, building a three-levelled dungeon out of the lid, bottom and an insert, to reveal progressive deeper levels of the dungeon

[Rating: 5/10] Move dragon, take tile, move dragon, give tile. Next player. Very quick. Not thematic at all, despite dragon miniature. Way too abstract and simple for my taste, but I guess it would be more strategic if everybody paed attention and knew what they were doing.
